newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-LOVE STILL HAUNTED BY LAST YEAR'S NEAR MISS AT U.S. OPEN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-LOVE STILL HAUNTED BY LAST YEAR'S NEAR MISS AT U.S. OPEN.

text.p: Davis Love remains one of the world's best golfers yet to win a major after coming so very close at last year's U.S. Open, a defeat that will haunt him the rest of his days.
"I think about that finish a lot," Love said about the climactic holes at Oakland Hills, where he finished bogey-bogey and one shot away from winner Steve Jones. "I always will."

Love, 33, has had great success on the U.S. tour, with 10 victories, and finished second at the 1995 Masters and tied for fourth at the 1995 U.S. Open before tying with British Open champion Tom Lehman behind Jones at last year's Open.
The time has seemed right for Love to add a major title to his resume, which makes the Oakland Hills memory linger.

Love missed the green at the penultimate hole, a par-3, and failed to get up-and-down for par. At the 18th, playing ahead of the final pairing of Jones and Lehman, Love left a slippery downhill birdie putt short by three feet and then slid his par putt past the edge of the cup.
"The finish was the most exciting finish I've ever been involved in," Love said on the eve of Thursday's start of this year's Open at Congressional Country Club.
A birdie at the 72nd hole at Oakland Hills would likely have given Love the Open title. Par would probably have put him in a playoff with Jones. The bogey dropped him into a funk.

"It took me a while to get to playing good again," said Love, who slumped after his disappointing Open finish. "I just wasn't playing with any confidence. My swing was still good. My putting stroke was still good. I just wasn't sharp."
Love has recovered his confidence and feels good about his prospects at the sprawling Congressional course.
"You couldn't draw one, I think, any better for a long hitter," he said. "If I can keep driving it like I've been driving it this year, the course will set up well for me."
Love believes the bitter past has better prepared him for an assault on a major.
"It's never going to go away (the disappointment), but it makes you more determined and makes you work harder," he said.
Victory this week would taste incredibly sweet to the likeable long-hitter, but would not remove the ache he still feels.
"If I win the Open Sunday, the first thing I'm going to think about Monday morning is, God, it could have been two in a row so easy."
"I could win 10 Opens, I'm still going to say that I lost a chance to win my 11th."
